Acts 7:5  He gave him no inheritance in it, not even a footstep’s space, but promised to give it to him as a possession and to his seed after him, although he had no child.
Acts 7:6  God spoke in this way: his seed would live as strangers in a foreign land, and they would enslave and mistreat them for four hundred years.
Acts 7:7  ‘But I will judge the nation they serve as slaves,’ God said, ‘and after these things they will come out and worship Me in this place.’
Acts 7:8  He gave him the covenant of circumcision. Thus Abraham fathered Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day; Isaac fathered Jacob, and Jacob the twelve patriarchs.
Acts 7:9  The patriarchs, jealous of Joseph, sold him into Egypt. But God was with him,
Acts 7:10  rescued him from all his afflictions, and gave him favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who appointed him ruler over Egypt and his whole household.
Acts 7:11  Famine came upon all Egypt and Canaan, with great affliction, and our fathers could find no provisions.
Acts 7:12  When Jacob heard that there was grain in Egypt, he sent our fathers there the first time.
Acts 7:13  On the second visit Joseph made himself known to his brothers, and Joseph’s family became known to Pharaoh.
Acts 7:14  Joseph sent and summoned his father Jacob and all his relatives, seventy-five persons in all.
Acts 7:15  Jacob went down to Egypt, and he and our fathers died.
Acts 7:16  They were brought over to Shechem and placed in the tomb Abraham had bought for a price in silver from the sons of Hamor in Shechem.
Acts 7:17  As the time of the promise God had declared to Abraham drew near, the people grew and multiplied in Egypt,
Acts 7:18  until another king arose over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
Acts 7:19  He dealt craftily with our people and mistreated our fathers, forcing them to expose their infants so that they would not be kept alive.
Acts 7:20  At that time Moses was born, and he was beautiful before God. He was brought up for three months in his father’s house.
Acts 7:21  When he was exposed, Pharaoh’s daughter took him up and brought him up as her own son.
Acts 7:22  Moses was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians and was powerful in his words and deeds.
Acts 7:23  When he reached the age of forty, it came into his heart to visit his brothers, the sons of Israel.
Acts 7:24  Seeing one of them being wronged, he defended him and avenged the oppressed man by striking down the Egyptian.
Acts 7:25  He supposed his brothers understood that God was giving them deliverance through his hand, but they did not understand.
Acts 7:26  The next day he came upon them as they were fighting and tried to reconcile them in peace, saying, ‘Men, you are brothers. Why are you wronging one another?’
Acts 7:27  But the one wronging his neighbor pushed him away and said, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge over us?
Acts 7:28  Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?’
Acts 7:29  At this saying Moses fled and became a stranger in the land of Midian, where he fathered two sons.
Acts 7:30  When forty years had passed, an angel appeared to him in the wilderness of Mount Sinai, in the flame of a burning bush.
Acts 7:31  When Moses saw it, he marveled at the sight. As he approached to examine it, the Lord’s voice came:
Acts 7:32  ‘I am the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob.’ Moses trembled and did not dare to look closely.
Acts 7:33  The Lord said to him, ‘Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.
Acts 7:34  I have indeed seen the mistreatment of My people in Egypt and heard their groaning, and I have come down to rescue them. Now come, let Me send you to Egypt.’
Acts 7:35  This Moses, whom they denied, saying, ‘Who appointed you ruler and judge?’—God has sent this very man as both ruler and redeemer, through the hand of the angel who appeared to him in the bush.
Acts 7:36  He led them out, doing wonders and signs in the land of Egypt, in the Red Sea, and in the wilderness for forty years.
Acts 7:37  This is the Moses who said to the sons of Israel, ‘God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers.’
Acts 7:38  He is the one who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers. He received living oracles to give to us,
Acts 7:39  but our fathers were unwilling to obey him. They pushed him away and turned in their hearts toward Egypt,
Acts 7:40  saying to Aaron, ‘Make us gods who will go before us. As for this Moses who led us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’
Acts 7:41  They made a calf in those days, offered sacrifice to the idol, and rejoiced in the works of their hands.
Acts 7:42  But God turned away and handed them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you offer Me slaughtered victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?
Acts 7:43  You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images you made to worship them. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.’
Acts 7:44  Our fathers had the Tent of Testimony in the wilderness, as the One who spoke to Moses directed him to make it according to the pattern he had seen.
Acts 7:45  Our fathers in their turn received it and brought it in with Joshua when they took possession of the nations’ land, whose people God drove out before our fathers. It remained until the days of David,
Acts 7:46  who found favor before God and asked to find a dwelling for the house of Jacob.
Acts 7:47  But Solomon built Him a house.
Acts 7:48  Yet the Most High does not dwell in things made by hands, as the prophet says:
Acts 7:49  ‘Heaven is My throne, and the earth the footstool of My feet. What kind of house will you build for Me, says the Lord, or what place is there for My rest?
Acts 7:50  Did not My hand make all these things?’
Acts 7:51  You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in hearts and ears! You always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you.
Acts 7:52  Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? They killed those who announced beforehand the coming of the Righteous One, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become—
Acts 7:53  you who received the law through the ordinances of angels and did not keep it.”
Acts 7:54  When they heard these things, they were cut to the heart with rage and ground their teeth at him.
Acts 7:55  But he, full of the Holy Spirit, gazed into heaven and saw the glory of God and Jesus standing at God’s right hand.
Acts 7:56  He said, “Look, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at God’s right hand.”
Acts 7:57  They cried out with a loud voice, stopped their ears, and rushed upon him together.
Acts 7:58  They drove him outside the city and began stoning him. The witnesses laid their garments at the feet of a young man called Saul.
Acts 7:59  They stoned Stephen as he called out, saying, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
Acts 7:60  Kneeling down, he cried with a loud voice, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” After saying this, he fell asleep.

Acts 8
Acts 8:1  Saul approved of his killing. That day a great persecution arose against the Church in Jerusalem, and all except the apostles were scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria.
Acts 8:2  Devout men buried Stephen and made great lamentation over him.
Acts 8:3  But Saul was ravaging the Church, entering house after house, dragging away both men and women, and handing them over to prison.
Acts 8:4  Those who were scattered went about proclaiming the word as good news.
Acts 8:5  Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed the Christ to them.
Acts 8:6  The crowds paid attention together to what Philip said, as they heard and saw the signs he was doing.
Acts 8:7  For unclean spirits came out of many who had them, crying with a loud voice, and many who were paralyzed or unable to walk were healed.
Acts 8:8  There was great joy in that city.
Acts 8:9  A man named Simon had previously practiced magic in the city and astonished the people of Samaria, claiming that he himself was someone great.
Acts 8:10  Everyone, from small to great, paid attention to him, saying, “This man is the Power of God that is called Great.”
Acts 8:11  They paid attention to him because he had astonished them with his magical practices for a long time.
Acts 8:12  But when they believed Philip as he proclaimed the good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, both men and women were baptized.
Acts 8:13  Simon himself also believed, and after being baptized he stayed close to Philip. Seeing signs and great works of power taking place, he was astonished.
Acts 8:14  When the apostles in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the word of God, they sent Peter and John to them.
Acts 8:15  They went down and prayed for them to receive the Holy Spirit,
Acts 8:16  for He had not yet fallen upon any of them; they had only been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Acts 8:17  Then they laid their hands upon them, and they received the Holy Spirit.
Acts 8:18  When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money,
Acts 8:19  saying, “Give me this authority too, so that anyone upon whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.”
Acts 8:20  But Peter said to him, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could acquire the gift of God with money!
Acts 8:21  You have neither part nor allotted share in this matter, for your heart is not upright before God.
Acts 8:22  Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and plead with the Lord that perhaps the intention of your heart may be forgiven you.
Acts 8:23  For I see that you are in bitter gall and a bond of unrighteousness.”
Acts 8:24  Simon answered, “You yourselves plead with the Lord for me, so that none of the things you have spoken may come upon me.”
Acts 8:25  After bearing solemn witness and speaking the word of the Lord, they returned toward Jerusalem, proclaiming the good news in many Samaritan villages.
Acts 8:26  An angel of the Lord spoke to Philip, saying, “Rise and go south to the road that descends from Jerusalem to Gaza.” This is a desert road.
Acts 8:27  He rose and went. And look—an Ethiopian man, a eunuch and an official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was over all her treasury, had come to Jerusalem to worship.
Acts 8:28  He was returning, seated in his chariot, and reading the prophet Isaiah.
Acts 8:29  The Spirit said to Philip, “Go near and join this chariot.”
Acts 8:30  Philip ran up, heard him reading Isaiah the prophet, and said, “Do you understand what you are reading?”
Acts 8:31  He said, “How could I, unless someone guides me?” And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
Acts 8:32  The passage of Scripture he was reading was this: “Like a sheep He was led to slaughter, and as a lamb is silent before its shearer, so He does not open His mouth.
Acts 8:33  In His humiliation His judgment was taken away. Who will recount His generation? For His life is taken from the earth.”
Acts 8:34  The eunuch said to Philip, “I ask you, about whom does the prophet say this—about himself or about someone else?”
Acts 8:35  Philip opened his mouth and, beginning from this Scripture, proclaimed to him the good news of Jesus.
Acts 8:36  As they went along the road, they came to some water, and the eunuch said, “Look, water! What prevents me from being baptized?”
Acts 8:38  He ordered the chariot to stop. Both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water, and Philip baptized him.
Acts 8:39  When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, for he went on his way rejoicing.
Acts 8:40  Philip was found at Azotus, and as he passed through, he proclaimed the good news in all the towns until he came to Caesarea.

Acts 9
Acts 9:1  Saul, still breathing threat and murder against the Lord’s disciples, went to the high priest
Acts 9:2  and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any belonging to the Way, both men and women, he might bring them bound to Jerusalem.
Acts 9:3  As he traveled and drew near Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him.
Acts 9:4  He fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?”
Acts 9:5  He said, “Who art Thou, Lord?” He answered, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
Acts 9:6  But rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
Acts 9:7  The men traveling with him stood speechless, hearing the voice but seeing no one.
Acts 9:8  Saul rose from the ground, but although his eyes were open, he could see nothing. They led him by the hand and brought him into Damascus.
Acts 9:9  For three days he could not see, and he neither ate nor drank.
Acts 9:10  There was a disciple in Damascus named Ananias. The Lord said to him in a vision, “Ananias.” He said, “Here I am, Lord.”
Acts 9:11  The Lord said to him, “Rise, go to the street called Straight, and seek in Judas’s house a man named Saul from Tarsus. Look, he is praying,
Acts 9:12  and in a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come in and lay hands upon him so that he may regain his sight.”
Acts 9:13  Ananias answered, “Lord, I have heard from many about this man, how much evil he has done to Thy saints in Jerusalem.
Acts 9:14  Here too he has authority from the chief priests to bind all who call upon Thy name.”
Acts 9:15  But the Lord said to him, “Go, for this man is a chosen vessel for Me, to carry My name before Gentiles and kings and the sons of Israel.
Acts 9:16  For I will show him how much he must suffer for My name.”
Acts 9:17  Ananias went and entered the house. Laying his hands upon him, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord has sent me—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you came—so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Acts 9:18  At once something like scales fell from his eyes, and he regained his sight. He rose and was baptized,
Acts 9:19  and after taking food he regained strength. He stayed for some days with the disciples in Damascus.
Acts 9:20  Immediately he proclaimed Jesus in the synagogues, saying, “He is the Son of God.”
Acts 9:21  All who heard him were astonished and said, “Is this not the one who devastated those in Jerusalem who call upon this name? And had he not come here for this purpose, to bring them bound before the chief priests?”
Acts 9:22  But Saul grew stronger and confounded the Jews living in Damascus by demonstrating that Jesus is the Christ.
Acts 9:23  After many days had passed, the Jews conspired to kill him,
Acts 9:24  but their plot became known to Saul. They were also watching the gates day and night to kill him.
Acts 9:25  His disciples took him by night and let him down through the wall, lowering him in a hamper.
Acts 9:26  When he arrived in Jerusalem, he tried to join the disciples, but they all feared him, not believing that he was a disciple.
Acts 9:27  Barnabas took him and brought him to the apostles. He related to them how Saul had seen the Lord on the road, how He had spoken to him, and how Saul had spoken boldly in Damascus in the name of Jesus.
Acts 9:28  He was with them, going in and out in Jerusalem and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord.
Acts 9:29  He spoke and disputed with the Hellenists, but they attempted to kill him.
Acts 9:30  When the brothers learned this, they brought him down to Caesarea and sent him away to Tarsus.
Acts 9:31  So the Church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace and was being built up. Walking in the fear of the Lord and in the encouragement of the Holy Spirit, it increased.
Acts 9:32  As Peter traveled among them all, he also went down to the saints who lived in Lydda.
Acts 9:33  There he found a man named Aeneas who had lain on a mat for eight years, for he was paralyzed.
Acts 9:34  Peter said to him, “Aeneas, Jesus Christ heals you. Rise and make your bed.” At once he rose.
Acts 9:35  All who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw him and turned to the Lord.
Acts 9:36  In Joppa there was a woman disciple named Tabitha, which translated is Dorcas. She was full of good works and acts of charity.
Acts 9:37  In those days she became ill and died. They washed her and laid her in an upper room.
Acts 9:38  Since Lydda was near Joppa, the disciples, hearing that Peter was there, sent two men to him, urging, “Do not delay in coming to us.”
Acts 9:39  Peter rose and went with them. When he arrived, they brought him into the upper room. All the widows stood beside him weeping and showing the tunics and garments Dorcas had made while she was with them.
Acts 9:40  Peter put everyone outside, knelt down, and prayed. Turning toward the body, he said, “Tabitha, rise.” She opened her eyes, saw Peter, and sat up.
Acts 9:41  He gave her his hand and raised her up. Then he called the saints and the widows and presented her alive.
Acts 9:42  This became known throughout Joppa, and many believed in the Lord.
Acts 9:43  He stayed in Joppa for many days with a certain Simon, a tanner.

Acts 10
Acts 10:1  In Caesarea there was a man named Cornelius, a centurion of the cohort called the Italian,
Acts 10:2  devout and fearing God with his whole household, giving many alms to the people and praying to God continually.
Acts 10:3  About the ninth hour of the day, he clearly saw in a vision an angel of God come in to him and say, “Cornelius.”
Acts 10:4  He stared at him in fear and said, “What is it, sir?” The angel said to him, “Your prayers and your alms have ascended as a memorial before God.
Acts 10:5  Now send men to Joppa and summon a certain Simon who is called Peter.
Acts 10:6  He is staying with a certain Simon, a tanner, whose house is beside the sea.”
Acts 10:7  When the angel who spoke to him had gone, Cornelius called two of his household slaves and a devout soldier from among those who attended him.
Acts 10:8  He explained everything to them and sent them to Joppa.
Acts 10:9  The next day, while they were traveling and approaching the city, Peter went up onto the roof to pray, about the sixth hour.
Acts 10:10  He became hungry and wanted to eat. While they were preparing the food, a trance came upon him.
Acts 10:11  He saw heaven opened and something like a large sheet descending, being lowered by its four corners to the earth.
Acts 10:12  In it were all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the sky.
Acts 10:13  A voice came to him: “Rise, Peter; slaughter and eat.”
Acts 10:14  Peter said, “By no means, Lord, for I have never eaten anything common and unclean.”
Acts 10:15  A voice came to him again, a second time: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”
Acts 10:16  This happened three times, and immediately the object was taken up into heaven.
Acts 10:17  While Peter was perplexed within himself about what the vision he had seen might mean, look—the men sent by Cornelius, having asked directions to Simon’s house, stood at the gate.
Acts 10:18  They called out and asked whether Simon, who was called Peter, was staying there.
Acts 10:19  While Peter was pondering the vision, the Spirit said to him, “Look, three men are seeking you.
Acts 10:20  Rise, go down, and go with them without hesitation, because I have sent them.”
Acts 10:21  Peter went down to the men and said, “I am the one you are seeking. What is the reason you have come?”
Acts 10:22  They said, “Cornelius, a centurion, a righteous and God-fearing man well spoken of by the whole Jewish nation, was directed by a holy angel to summon you to his house and hear words from you.”
Acts 10:23  So he invited them in and gave them lodging. The next day he rose and went away with them, and some of the brothers from Joppa accompanied him.
Acts 10:24  The following day he entered Caesarea. Cornelius was expecting them and had called together his relatives and close friends.
Acts 10:25  As Peter was about to enter, Cornelius met him, fell at his feet, and bowed before him.
Acts 10:26  But Peter raised him up, saying, “Rise; I too am a human being.”
Acts 10:27  While speaking with him, Peter entered and found many people gathered.
Acts 10:28  He said to them, “You know how forbidden it is for a Jewish man to associate with or visit someone of another people. Yet God has shown me to call no human being common or unclean.
Acts 10:29  Therefore I came without objection when summoned. So I ask, for what reason did you send for me?”
Acts 10:30  Cornelius said, “Four days ago, at this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour, and look—a man stood before me in shining clothing.
Acts 10:31  He said, ‘Cornelius, your prayer has been heard, and your alms have been remembered before God.
Acts 10:32  Send, therefore, to Joppa and summon Simon who is called Peter. He is staying in the house of Simon the tanner beside the sea.’
Acts 10:33  So I sent to you at once, and you have done well to come. Now we are all here before God to hear everything the Lord has commanded you.”
Acts 10:34  Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I understand that God shows no partiality,
Acts 10:35  but in every nation, whoever fears Him and practices righteousness is acceptable to Him.
Acts 10:36  He sent the word to the sons of Israel, proclaiming good news of peace through Jesus Christ—He is Lord of all.
Acts 10:37  You know what took place throughout all Judea, beginning from Galilee after the baptism John proclaimed:
Acts 10:38  Jesus of Nazareth—how God anointed Him with the Holy Spirit and power. He went about doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, because God was with Him.
Acts 10:39  We are witnesses of everything He did both in the country of the Jews and in Jerusalem. They also killed Him by hanging Him on a tree.
Acts 10:40  God raised Him on the third day and granted that He should appear,
Acts 10:41  not to all the people, but to witnesses chosen beforehand by God—to us, who ate and drank with Him after He rose from the dead.
Acts 10:42  He commanded us to proclaim to the people and bear solemn witness that He is the One appointed by God as judge of the living and the dead.
Acts 10:43  All the prophets bear witness to Him: everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins through His name.”
Acts 10:44  While Peter was still speaking these words, the Holy Spirit fell upon all who were hearing the message.
Acts 10:45  The believers from the circumcision who had come with Peter were astonished that the gift of the Holy Spirit had been poured out even upon the Gentiles,
Acts 10:46  for they heard them speaking in tongues and magnifying God. Then Peter said,
Acts 10:47  “Can anyone withhold the water so that these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have, should not be baptized?”
Acts 10:48  He ordered them to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ. Then they asked him to stay for some days.

Acts 11
Acts 11:1  The apostles and the brothers throughout Judea heard that the Gentiles too had received the word of God.
Acts 11:2  When Peter went up to Jerusalem, those of the circumcision disputed with him,
Acts 11:3  saying, “You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them.”
Acts 11:4  Peter began explaining to them in order, saying,
Acts 11:5  “I was in the city of Joppa praying, and in a trance I saw a vision: something like a large sheet descending, lowered by its four corners from heaven, and it came right to me.
Acts 11:6  I looked intently into it and examined it, and I saw the four-footed animals of the earth, wild animals, creeping things, and birds of the sky.
Acts 11:7  I also heard a voice saying to me, ‘Rise, Peter; slaughter and eat.’
Acts 11:8  But I said, ‘By no means, Lord, for nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth.’
Acts 11:9  A voice answered a second time from heaven, ‘What God has cleansed, you must not call common.’
Acts 11:10  This happened three times, and everything was drawn up again into heaven.
Acts 11:11  And look, at once three men stood at the house where we were, sent to me from Caesarea.
Acts 11:12  The Spirit told me to go with them, making no distinction. These six brothers also went with me, and we entered the man’s house.
Acts 11:13  He reported to us how he had seen the angel standing in his house and saying, ‘Send to Joppa and summon Simon who is called Peter,
Acts 11:14  who will speak words to you by which you and your whole household will be saved.’
Acts 11:15  As I began to speak, the Holy Spirit fell upon them just as upon us at the beginning.
Acts 11:16  I remembered the Lord’s word, how He said, ‘John baptized with water, but you will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.’
Acts 11:17  If, then, God gave them the same gift as He gave us when we believed in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was I that I could hinder God?”
Acts 11:18  When they heard these things, they fell silent and glorified God, saying, “Then God has granted even the Gentiles repentance leading to life.”
Acts 11:19  Those who had been scattered by the affliction that arose over Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews alone.
Acts 11:20  But some of them were men from Cyprus and Cyrene who came to Antioch and also spoke to the Hellenists, proclaiming the good news of the Lord Jesus.
Acts 11:21  The Lord’s hand was with them, and a great number believed and turned to the Lord.
Acts 11:22  The report about them reached the ears of the Church in Jerusalem, and they sent Barnabas to travel as far as Antioch.
Acts 11:23  When he arrived and saw the grace of God, he rejoiced and encouraged them all to remain with the Lord with steadfast purpose of heart,
Acts 11:24  for he was a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and faith. A considerable crowd was added to the Lord.
Acts 11:25  He went away to Tarsus to search for Saul,
Acts 11:26  and when he found him, he brought him to Antioch. For a whole year they gathered with the Church and taught a considerable crowd. It was in Antioch that the disciples were first called Christians.
Acts 11:27  In those days prophets came down from Jerusalem to Antioch.
Acts 11:28  One of them, named Agabus, stood up and indicated through the Spirit that a great famine would come over the whole inhabited world. This happened in the time of Claudius.
Acts 11:29  The disciples determined, each according to his means, to send relief to the brothers living in Judea.
Acts 11:30  This they did, sending it to the elders by the hand of Barnabas and Saul.

Acts 12
Acts 12:1  About that time King Herod laid hands on some of the Church to mistreat them.
Acts 12:2  He killed James, the brother of John, with the sword.
Acts 12:3  When he saw that this pleased the Jews, he proceeded to arrest Peter as well. These were the days of Unleavened Bread.
Acts 12:4  He seized him and put him in prison, handing him over to four squads of four soldiers to guard him, intending to bring him out before the people after the Passover.
Acts 12:5  So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was being made to God by the Church.
Acts 12:6  On the night before Herod was to bring him out, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while guards before the door kept watch over the prison.
Acts 12:7  And look—an angel of the Lord stood beside him, and light shone in the cell. Striking Peter’s side, he woke him and said, “Rise quickly.” The chains fell from his hands.
Acts 12:8  The angel said to him, “Fasten your belt and put on your sandals.” He did so. Then he said to him, “Wrap your cloak around you and follow me.”
Acts 12:9  Peter went out and followed. He did not know that what was happening through the angel was real; he thought he was seeing a vision.
Acts 12:10  They passed the first guard post and the second and came to the iron gate leading into the city. It opened for them of its own accord. They went out and continued along one street, and immediately the angel left him.
Acts 12:11  When Peter came to himself, he said, “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me from Herod’s hand and from everything the Jewish people were expecting.”
Acts 12:12  After considering this, he went to the house of Mary, the mother of John who was called Mark, where many had gathered and were praying.
Acts 12:13  When he knocked at the outer gate’s door, a slave girl named Rhoda came to answer.
Acts 12:14  Recognizing Peter’s voice, in her joy she did not open the gate, but ran inside and announced that Peter was standing before it.
Acts 12:15  They said to her, “You are out of your mind.” But she insisted that it was so. They said, “It is his angel.”
Acts 12:16  Peter kept knocking. When they opened the door, they saw him and were astonished.
Acts 12:17  He motioned with his hand for them to be silent and related how the Lord had brought him out of prison. He said, “Report these things to James and the brothers.” Then he left and went to another place.
Acts 12:18  When day came, there was no small disturbance among the soldiers over what had become of Peter.
Acts 12:19  Herod searched for him and did not find him. After examining the guards, he ordered them to be led away for execution. Then he went down from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.
Acts 12:20  Herod was fiercely hostile toward the people of Tyre and Sidon. They came to him with one accord and, after winning over Blastus, the king’s chamberlain, asked for peace, because their country received its food from the king’s territory.
Acts 12:21  On an appointed day Herod put on royal clothing, sat on the tribunal, and delivered an address to them.
Acts 12:22  The populace shouted, “A god’s voice, and not a human being’s!”
Acts 12:23  Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him because he did not give the glory to God. He was eaten by worms and breathed his last.
Acts 12:24  But the word of God grew and multiplied.
Acts 12:25  Barnabas and Saul returned to Jerusalem after completing their service, and took along John who was called Mark.

Acts 13
Acts 13:1  In the Church at Antioch there were prophets and teachers: Barnabas, Simeon who was called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch, and Saul.
Acts 13:2  While they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, “Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.”
Acts 13:3  Then, after fasting and praying and laying their hands upon them, they sent them away.
Acts 13:4  So, sent out by the Holy Spirit, they went down to Seleucia and from there sailed to Cyprus.
Acts 13:5  When they came to Salamis, they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. They also had John as an assistant.
Acts 13:6  They traveled through the whole island as far as Paphos and found a certain magician, a Jewish false prophet named Bar-Jesus,
Acts 13:7  who was with the proconsul Sergius Paulus, an intelligent man. The proconsul summoned Barnabas and Saul and sought to hear the word of God.
Acts 13:8  But Elymas the magician—for that is how his name is translated—opposed them, seeking to turn the proconsul away from the faith.
Acts 13:9  Saul, who was also called Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, looked intently at him
Acts 13:10  and said, “You who are full of all deceit and all villainy, son of the devil, enemy of all righteousness—will you not stop making crooked the Lord’s straight ways?
Acts 13:11  Now look, the Lord’s hand is upon you, and you will be blind, unable to see the sun for a time.” Immediately mist and darkness fell upon him, and he went about seeking people to lead him by the hand.
Acts 13:12  When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord.
Acts 13:13  Paul and his companions sailed from Paphos and came to Perga in Pamphylia. John left them and returned to Jerusalem.
Acts 13:14  They continued from Perga and arrived at Pisidian Antioch. On the Sabbath day they entered the synagogue and sat down.
Acts 13:15  After the reading of the law and the prophets, the synagogue rulers sent word to them, saying, “Men, brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, speak.”
Acts 13:16  Paul rose, motioned with his hand, and said, “Men of Israel and you who fear God, listen.
Acts 13:17  The God of this people Israel chose our fathers and exalted the people during their stay as strangers in the land of Egypt. With an uplifted arm He led them out of it,
Acts 13:18  and for about forty years He put up with their conduct in the wilderness.
Acts 13:19  He overthrew seven nations in the land of Canaan and gave their land as an inheritance,
Acts 13:20  over about four hundred and fifty years. After these things He gave judges until Samuel the prophet.
Acts 13:21  Then they asked for a king, and God gave them Saul son of Kish, a man of the tribe of Benjamin, for forty years.
Acts 13:22  After removing him, He raised up David as king for them, to whom He also bore witness, saying, ‘I have found David son of Jesse, a man after My heart, who will do all My will.’
Acts 13:23  From this man’s seed, according to promise, God brought Israel a Savior, Jesus,
Acts 13:24  after John had proclaimed, before His coming, a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel.
Acts 13:25  As John was completing his course, he said, ‘Who do you think I am? I am not that one. But look, One is coming after me, whose sandals I am not worthy to untie.’
Acts 13:26  Men, brothers, sons of Abraham’s family, and those among you who fear God: to us the message of this salvation has been sent.
Acts 13:27  For those living in Jerusalem and their rulers, failing to recognize Him and the voices of the prophets read every Sabbath, fulfilled those voices by condemning Him.
Acts 13:28  Although they found no cause for death, they asked Pilate to have Him killed.
Acts 13:29  When they had completed everything written about Him, they took Him down from the tree and laid Him in a tomb.
Acts 13:30  But God raised Him from the dead.
Acts 13:31  For many days He appeared to those who had gone up with Him from Galilee to Jerusalem, who are now His witnesses to the people.
Acts 13:32  We proclaim to you the good news of the promise made to the fathers:
Acts 13:33  God has fulfilled this for us, their children, by raising up Jesus, as it is also written in the second psalm: ‘Thou art My Son; today I have begotten Thee.’
Acts 13:34  God has spoken this way about raising Him from the dead, never again to return to decay: ‘I will give you the holy and sure blessings of David.’
Acts 13:35  Therefore He also says in another place, ‘Thou wilt not allow Thy Holy One to see decay.’
Acts 13:36  For David, after serving his own generation according to God’s purpose, fell asleep, was gathered to his fathers, and saw decay.
Acts 13:37  But the One whom God raised did not see decay.
Acts 13:38  Therefore let it be known to you, men, brothers, that through Him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you; and from everything from which you could not be justified in the law of Moses,
Acts 13:39  in Him everyone who believes is justified.
Acts 13:40  Take care, then, lest what is spoken in the prophets come upon you:
Acts 13:41  ‘Look, you scoffers, marvel and vanish, for I am doing a work in your days, a work you will never believe even if someone recounts it to you.’”
Acts 13:42  As they went out, the people urged that these words be spoken to them on the next Sabbath.
Acts 13:43  After the synagogue gathering was dismissed, many Jews and devout converts followed Paul and Barnabas, who spoke with them and urged them to remain in the grace of God.
Acts 13:44  On the coming Sabbath, almost the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord.
Acts 13:45  When the Jews saw the crowds, they were filled with jealousy and contradicted what Paul was saying, speaking abusively.
Acts 13:46  Paul and Barnabas spoke boldly and said, “It was necessary for God’s word to be spoken to you first. Since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, look—we are turning to the Gentiles.
Acts 13:47  For the Lord has commanded us in this way: ‘I have appointed you as a light for Gentiles, so that you may bring salvation to the end of the earth.’”
Acts 13:48  When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and glorified the word of the Lord, and as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed.
Acts 13:49  The word of the Lord spread through the whole region.
Acts 13:50  But the Jews stirred up the devout women of high standing and the leading men of the city, raised persecution against Paul and Barnabas, and drove them out of their territory.
Acts 13:51  They shook the dust from their feet against them and went to Iconium.
Acts 13:52  The disciples were filled with joy and the Holy Spirit.

Acts 14
Acts 14:1  In Iconium they entered the Jewish synagogue together and spoke in such a way that a great multitude of both Jews and Greeks believed.
Acts 14:2  But the Jews who refused to believe stirred up the Gentiles and embittered their minds against the brothers.
Acts 14:3  So they stayed a considerable time, speaking boldly in reliance on the Lord, who bore witness to the word of His grace by granting signs and wonders to take place through their hands.
Acts 14:4  The people of the city were divided: some sided with the Jews and others with the apostles.
Acts 14:5  When an attempt was made by both Gentiles and Jews, together with their rulers, to mistreat and stone them,
Acts 14:6  they learned of it and fled to Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, and the surrounding region.
Acts 14:7  There they continued proclaiming the good news.
Acts 14:8  In Lystra a man was sitting who had no strength in his feet, unable to walk from his mother’s womb; he had never walked.
Acts 14:9  He listened to Paul speaking. Paul looked intently at him and saw that he had faith to be made well,
Acts 14:10  and said with a loud voice, “Stand upright on your feet.” He leaped up and began walking.
Acts 14:11  When the crowds saw what Paul had done, they raised their voice, saying in Lycaonian, “The gods have come down to us in human likeness.”
Acts 14:12  They called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, because he was the leading speaker.
Acts 14:13  The priest of Zeus, whose shrine was before the city, brought bulls and garlands to the gates and wanted to offer sacrifice with the crowds.
Acts 14:14  When the apostles Barnabas and Paul heard this, they tore their garments and rushed out into the crowd, crying out
Acts 14:15  and saying, “Men, why are you doing these things? We too are human beings, of the same nature as you. We proclaim good news to you: turn from these worthless things to the living God, who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything in them.
Acts 14:16  In past generations He allowed all the nations to go their own ways.
Acts 14:17  Yet He did not leave Himself without witness in doing good, giving you rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness.”
Acts 14:18  Even by saying these things, they scarcely stopped the crowds from sacrificing to them.
Acts 14:19  Jews came from Antioch and Iconium, persuaded the crowds, stoned Paul, and dragged him outside the city, supposing he was dead.
Acts 14:20  But when the disciples surrounded him, he rose and entered the city. The next day he went with Barnabas to Derbe.
Acts 14:21  After proclaiming the good news to that city and making many disciples, they returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch,
Acts 14:22  strengthening the souls of the disciples, encouraging them to remain in the faith, and saying, “Through many afflictions we must enter the kingdom of God.”
Acts 14:23  They appointed elders for them in each Church and, after praying with fasting, entrusted them to the Lord in whom they had believed.
Acts 14:24  They passed through Pisidia and came to Pamphylia.
Acts 14:25  After speaking the word in Perga, they went down to Attalia.
Acts 14:26  From there they sailed to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to the grace of God for the work they had now completed.
Acts 14:27  When they arrived and gathered the Church, they reported all that God had done with them and how He had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.
Acts 14:28  They stayed quite a long time with the disciples.

Acts 15
Acts 15:1  Some men came down from Judea and taught the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.”
Acts 15:2  When Paul and Barnabas had a serious disagreement and debate with them, they appointed Paul and Barnabas and some others from among them to go up to the apostles and elders in Jerusalem about this question.
Acts 15:3  Sent on their way by the Church, they passed through Phoenicia and Samaria, recounting the conversion of the Gentiles and bringing great joy to all the brothers.
Acts 15:4  When they arrived in Jerusalem, they were welcomed by the Church, the apostles, and the elders, and reported all that God had done with them.
Acts 15:5  But some believers from the party of the Pharisees rose and said, “It is necessary to circumcise them and command them to keep the law of Moses.”
Acts 15:6  The apostles and the elders gathered to consider this matter.
Acts 15:7  After much debate, Peter rose and said to them, “Men, brothers, you know that in earlier days God made a choice among you, that through my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the good news and believe.
Acts 15:8  God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them by giving them the Holy Spirit just as He did to us.
Acts 15:9  He made no distinction between us and them, cleansing their hearts by faith.
Acts 15:10  Now, therefore, why are you testing God by placing upon the disciples’ neck a yoke that neither our fathers nor we were able to bear?
Acts 15:11  Rather, we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, in the same way as they are.”
Acts 15:12  The whole multitude became silent and listened to Barnabas and Paul relate all the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.
Acts 15:13  After they fell silent, James spoke: “Men, brothers, listen to me.
Acts 15:14  Simeon has related how God first visited the Gentiles to take from them a people for His name.
Acts 15:15  With this the words of the prophets agree, as it is written:
Acts 15:16  ‘After these things I will return and rebuild David’s fallen tent. I will rebuild its ruins and set it upright,
Acts 15:17  so that the remnant of humankind and all the nations over whom My name has been called may seek the Lord, says the Lord, who makes these things
Acts 15:18  known from long ago.’
Acts 15:19  Therefore I judge that we should not trouble those from the Gentiles who are turning to God,
Acts 15:20  but should write to them to abstain from the pollutions of idols, sexual immorality, what is strangled, and blood.
Acts 15:21  For since ancient times, people in every city have proclaimed Moses, and he is read in the synagogues every Sabbath.”
Acts 15:22  Then the apostles and elders, with the whole Church, decided to choose men from among them and send them to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas: Judas called Barsabbas, and Silas, leading men among the brothers.
Acts 15:23  They wrote by their hand: “The apostles and elders, your brothers, to the brothers from the Gentiles in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia: greetings.
Acts 15:24  Since we have heard that some who went out from among us troubled you with words, unsettling your souls, although we gave them no instruction,
Acts 15:25  we have decided with one accord to choose men and send them to you with our beloved Barnabas and Paul,
Acts 15:26  men who have given over their lives for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Acts 15:27  We have therefore sent Judas and Silas, who will themselves report the same things by word of mouth.
Acts 15:28  For it seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to place no further burden upon you except these necessary things:
Acts 15:29  to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, blood, things strangled, and sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.”
Acts 15:30  After being sent off, they went down to Antioch, gathered the multitude, and delivered the letter.
Acts 15:31  When they read it, they rejoiced at its encouragement.
Acts 15:32  Judas and Silas, themselves also prophets, encouraged the brothers with many words and strengthened them.
Acts 15:33  After spending some time there, they were sent away in peace by the brothers to those who had sent them.
Acts 15:35  Paul and Barnabas remained in Antioch, teaching and proclaiming the word of the Lord as good news, along with many others.
Acts 15:36  After some days Paul said to Barnabas, “Let us return and visit the brothers in every city where we proclaimed the word of the Lord, to see how they are.”
Acts 15:37  Barnabas wanted to take along John, who was called Mark, as well.
Acts 15:38  But Paul considered it right not to take along the man who had withdrawn from them in Pamphylia and had not gone with them to the work.
Acts 15:39  A sharp disagreement arose, so that they separated from one another. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus,
Acts 15:40  but Paul chose Silas and departed, entrusted by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
Acts 15:41  He traveled through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the Churches.

Acts 16
Acts 16:1  He also came to Derbe and Lystra. There was a disciple there named Timothy, the son of a believing Jewish woman, but of a Greek father.
Acts 16:2  He was well spoken of by the brothers in Lystra and Iconium.
Acts 16:3  Paul wanted him to go with him, and took him and circumcised him because of the Jews in those places, for they all knew that his father was Greek.
Acts 16:4  As they traveled through the cities, they handed on to them for observance the decisions made by the apostles and elders in Jerusalem.
Acts 16:5  So the Churches were strengthened in the faith and increased in number each day.
Acts 16:6  They passed through Phrygia and the Galatian region, having been prevented by the Holy Spirit from speaking the word in Asia.
Acts 16:7  When they came near Mysia, they tried to go into Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not permit them.
Acts 16:8  Passing by Mysia, they went down to Troas.
Acts 16:9  During the night a vision appeared to Paul: a Macedonian man was standing and urging him, saying, “Cross over to Macedonia and help us.”
Acts 16:10  When he had seen the vision, we immediately sought to go out to Macedonia, concluding that God had called us to proclaim the good news to them.
Acts 16:11  We sailed from Troas and made a straight course to Samothrace, and on the next day to Neapolis,
Acts 16:12  and from there to Philippi, a city of the first district of Macedonia and a colony. We stayed in that city for some days.
Acts 16:13  On the Sabbath day we went outside the gate beside a river, where we thought there was a place of prayer. We sat down and spoke to the women who had gathered.
Acts 16:14  A woman named Lydia, a seller of purple goods from the city of Thyatira, who worshiped God, was listening. The Lord opened her heart to attend to what Paul was saying.
Acts 16:15  After she and her household were baptized, she urged us, saying, “If you have judged me faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay.” And she prevailed upon us.
Acts 16:16  As we were going to the place of prayer, a slave girl with a spirit of divination met us. She brought her masters much profit by fortune-telling.
Acts 16:17  She followed Paul and us, crying out, “These men are servants of God Most High, who proclaim to you the way of salvation.”
Acts 16:18  She kept doing this for many days. Paul, greatly troubled, turned and said to the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” It came out that very hour.
Acts 16:19  When her masters saw that their hope of profit had gone out, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them into the marketplace before the rulers.
Acts 16:20  They brought them before the magistrates and said, “These men are throwing our city into turmoil. They are Jews,
Acts 16:21  and they proclaim customs that we, being Romans, are not permitted to accept or practice.”
Acts 16:22  The crowd joined the attack against them. The magistrates tore off their garments and ordered them to be beaten with rods.
Acts 16:23  After inflicting many blows on them, they threw them into prison and ordered the jailer to keep them securely.
Acts 16:24  Having received such an order, he put them in the inner prison and secured their feet in the stocks.
Acts 16:25  About midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, while the prisoners listened to them.
Acts 16:26  Suddenly there was a great earthquake, so that the jail’s foundations were shaken. At once all the doors opened, and everyone’s bonds were loosened.
Acts 16:27  The jailer awoke and saw the prison doors open. He drew his sword and was about to kill himself, supposing the prisoners had escaped.
Acts 16:28  But Paul cried with a loud voice, “Do yourself no harm, for we are all here.”
Acts 16:29  He called for lights, rushed inside, and fell trembling before Paul and Silas.
Acts 16:30  He brought them outside and said, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?”
Acts 16:31  They said, “Believe in the Lord Jesus, and you will be saved, you and your household.”
Acts 16:32  They spoke the word of the Lord to him, together with all who were in his house.
Acts 16:33  At that very hour of the night he took them and washed their wounds. Immediately he and all his people were baptized.
Acts 16:34  He brought them up into his house, set food before them, and rejoiced with his whole household, having believed in God.
Acts 16:35  When day came, the magistrates sent the officers, saying, “Release those men.”
Acts 16:36  The jailer reported these words to Paul: “The magistrates have sent word for you to be released. Now come out and go in peace.”
Acts 16:37  But Paul said to them, “They beat us publicly without a verdict, although we are Roman citizens, and threw us into prison. And now are they sending us away secretly? No indeed! Let them come themselves and lead us out.”
Acts 16:38  The officers reported these words to the magistrates, and they were afraid when they heard that the men were Romans.
Acts 16:39  They came and appealed to them, led them out, and asked them to leave the city.
Acts 16:40  After leaving the prison, they went to Lydia’s house. They saw the brothers, encouraged them, and departed.

Acts 17
Acts 17:1  After traveling through Amphipolis and Apollonia, they came to Thessalonica, where there was a Jewish synagogue.
Acts 17:2  As was his custom, Paul went in to them, and for three Sabbaths he reasoned with them from the Scriptures,
Acts 17:3  explaining and setting before them that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead, and saying, “This Jesus whom I proclaim to you is the Christ.”
Acts 17:4  Some of them were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas, as did a great multitude of devout Greeks and not a few of the leading women.
Acts 17:5  But the Jews became jealous and took some wicked men from the marketplace, gathered a mob, and threw the city into turmoil. They attacked Jason’s house and sought to bring Paul and Silas out to the populace.
Acts 17:6  When they did not find them, they dragged Jason and some brothers before the city officials, shouting, “These men who have upset the inhabited world have come here too,
Acts 17:7  and Jason has welcomed them. They all act against Caesar’s decrees, saying that there is another king, Jesus.”
Acts 17:8  They disturbed the crowd and the city officials who heard these things.
Acts 17:9  After taking security from Jason and the others, the officials released them.
Acts 17:10  The brothers immediately sent Paul and Silas away by night to Berea. When they arrived, they went into the Jewish synagogue.
Acts 17:11  These people were more noble-minded than those in Thessalonica: they welcomed the word with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
Acts 17:12  Many of them therefore believed, as did not a few Greek women of high standing and men.
Acts 17:13  But when the Jews from Thessalonica learned that the word of God had also been proclaimed by Paul in Berea, they came there too, stirring up and disturbing the crowds.
Acts 17:14  Then the brothers immediately sent Paul away to go as far as the sea, while Silas and Timothy remained there.
Acts 17:15  Those escorting Paul brought him as far as Athens. After receiving an order for Silas and Timothy to come to him as quickly as possible, they departed.
Acts 17:16  While Paul waited for them in Athens, his spirit was provoked within him as he observed that the city was full of idols.
Acts 17:17  So he reasoned in the synagogue with the Jews and the worshipers, and in the marketplace every day with those who happened to be there.
Acts 17:18  Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also engaged him. Some said, “What is this babbler trying to say?” Others said, “He seems to be a proclaimer of foreign divinities,” because he proclaimed the good news of Jesus and the resurrection.
Acts 17:19  They took him and brought him to the Areopagus, saying, “May we know what this new teaching is that you are speaking?
Acts 17:20  For you are bringing some strange things to our ears. We therefore wish to know what these things mean.”
Acts 17:21  Now all the Athenians and the foreigners staying there spent their free time doing nothing but telling or hearing the latest thing.
Acts 17:22  Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and said, “Men of Athens, I perceive that in every respect you are very religious.
Acts 17:23  For as I passed through and observed your objects of worship, I also found an altar inscribed, ‘To an unknown god.’ What you worship without knowing, this I proclaim to you.
Acts 17:24  The God who made the world and everything in it, being Lord of heaven and earth, does not dwell in sanctuaries made by hands.
Acts 17:25  Nor is He served by human hands as though He needed anything, since He Himself gives everyone life and breath and everything.
Acts 17:26  From one He made every nation of humanity to live upon the whole face of the earth, determining their appointed times and the boundaries of their dwelling,
Acts 17:27  so that they might seek God, if perhaps they might feel their way toward Him and find Him, though He is not far from each one of us.
Acts 17:28  For in Him we live and move and exist, as even some of your own poets have said, ‘For we too are His offspring.’
Acts 17:29  Since we are God’s offspring, we ought not to think that the divine nature is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by human art and thought.
Acts 17:30  Therefore, having overlooked the times of ignorance, God now commands all people everywhere to repent,
Acts 17:31  because He has fixed a day on which He will judge the inhabited world in righteousness through a Man whom He appointed, giving assurance to everyone by raising Him from the dead.”
Acts 17:32  When they heard of a resurrection of the dead, some mocked, while others said, “We will hear you again about this.”
Acts 17:33  So Paul went out from their midst.
Acts 17:34  But some people joined him and believed, among them Dionysius the Areopagite, a woman named Damaris, and others with them.

Acts 18
Acts 18:1  After these things he left Athens and came to Corinth.
Acts 18:2  He found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla, because Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to them,
Acts 18:3  and because he practiced the same trade, he stayed with them and worked, for they were tentmakers by trade.
Acts 18:4  Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue and sought to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
Acts 18:5  When Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself to the word, bearing solemn witness to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ.
Acts 18:6  When they opposed him and spoke abusively, he shook out his garments and said to them, “Your blood be upon your own heads. I am clean. From now on I will go to the Gentiles.”
Acts 18:7  He left there and entered the house of a man named Titius Justus, a worshiper of God, whose house was next to the synagogue.
Acts 18:8  Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believed in the Lord with his whole household. Many of the Corinthians who heard believed and were baptized.
Acts 18:9  The Lord said to Paul by a vision in the night, “Do not fear, but speak and do not be silent,
Acts 18:10  because I am with you, and no one will attack you to harm you, for I have many people in this city.”
Acts 18:11  He stayed a year and six months, teaching the word of God among them.
Acts 18:12  While Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, the Jews rose together against Paul and brought him before the tribunal,
Acts 18:13  saying, “This man persuades people to worship God contrary to the law.”
Acts 18:14  As Paul was about to open his mouth, Gallio said to the Jews, “If it were some wrongdoing or wicked crime, O Jews, I would have reason to hear you out.
Acts 18:15  But if these are questions about a word, names, and your own law, see to it yourselves. I do not wish to be a judge of these things.”
Acts 18:16  He drove them away from the tribunal.
Acts 18:17  They all seized Sosthenes, the synagogue ruler, and beat him before the tribunal. Gallio cared about none of these things.
Acts 18:18  Paul stayed many more days, then took leave of the brothers and sailed for Syria, with Priscilla and Aquila. He had cut his hair at Cenchreae, for he had a vow.
Acts 18:19  They arrived at Ephesus, and he left them there. He himself entered the synagogue and reasoned with the Jews.
Acts 18:20  When they asked him to stay for a longer time, he did not agree.
Acts 18:21  Instead, he took leave of them, saying, “I will return to you again, God willing,” and sailed from Ephesus.
Acts 18:22  He landed at Caesarea, went up and greeted the Church, and went down to Antioch.
Acts 18:23  After spending some time there, he departed and traveled from place to place through the Galatian region and Phrygia, strengthening all the disciples.
Acts 18:24  A Jew named Apollos, a native of Alexandria, came to Ephesus. He was an eloquent man, powerful in the Scriptures.
Acts 18:25  He had been instructed in the way of the Lord, and being fervent in spirit, he spoke and taught accurately the things concerning Jesus, though he knew only John’s baptism.
Acts 18:26  He began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more accurately.
Acts 18:27  When he wished to cross over to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him and wrote to the disciples to welcome him. On arriving, he greatly helped those who had believed through grace,
Acts 18:28  for he vigorously refuted the Jews in public, demonstrating through the Scriptures that Jesus is the Christ.

Acts 19
Acts 19:1  While Apollos was in Corinth, Paul passed through the upper regions and came down to Ephesus. He found some disciples
Acts 19:2  and said to them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They said to him, “We have not even heard whether there is a Holy Spirit.”
Acts 19:3  He said, “Into what, then, were you baptized?” They said, “Into John’s baptism.”
Acts 19:4  Paul said, “John baptized with a baptism of repentance, telling the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus.”
Acts 19:5  When they heard this, they were baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus.
Acts 19:6  When Paul laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit came upon them, and they spoke in tongues and prophesied.
Acts 19:7  There were about twelve men in all.
Acts 19:8  He entered the synagogue and spoke boldly for three months, reasoning and persuading concerning the kingdom of God.
Acts 19:9  But when some became hardened and refused to believe, speaking evil of the Way before the multitude, he withdrew from them and separated the disciples, reasoning daily in the lecture hall of Tyrannus.
Acts 19:10  This continued for two years, so that all who lived in Asia heard the word of the Lord, both Jews and Greeks.
Acts 19:11  God was doing extraordinary mighty works through Paul’s hands,
Acts 19:12  so that even cloths or aprons from contact with his skin were carried to the sick, and their diseases left them and the evil spirits went out.
Acts 19:13  Some itinerant Jewish exorcists also attempted to invoke the name of the Lord Jesus over those who had evil spirits, saying, “I solemnly charge you by the Jesus whom Paul proclaims.”
Acts 19:14  Seven sons of a certain Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, were doing this.
Acts 19:15  But the evil spirit answered them, “Jesus I know, and Paul I recognize, but who are you?”
Acts 19:16  The man in whom the evil spirit was leaped upon them, mastered both of them, and overpowered them, so that they fled from that house naked and wounded.
Acts 19:17  This became known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. Fear fell upon them all, and the name of the Lord Jesus was magnified.
Acts 19:18  Many who had believed came, confessing and reporting their practices.
Acts 19:19  A considerable number who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them before everyone. They calculated their prices and found the total to be fifty thousand in silver.
Acts 19:20  In this way the word of the Lord grew mightily and prevailed.
Acts 19:21  After these things were completed, Paul resolved in spirit to pass through Macedonia and Achaia and go to Jerusalem, saying, “After I have been there, I must also see Rome.”
Acts 19:22  He sent two of those who assisted him, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself remained in Asia for a time.
Acts 19:23  About that time a serious disturbance arose concerning the Way.
Acts 19:24  A silversmith named Demetrius, who made silver shrines of Artemis, provided considerable business for the craftsmen.
Acts 19:25  He gathered them and the workers in related trades and said, “Men, you know that our prosperity comes from this business.
Acts 19:26  You see and hear that not only in Ephesus but in almost all Asia this Paul has persuaded and turned away a considerable crowd, saying that things made by hands are not gods.
Acts 19:27  There is danger not only that this trade of ours will fall into disrepute, but also that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be reckoned as nothing, and that she whom all Asia and the inhabited world worship will be stripped of her magnificence.”
Acts 19:28  When they heard this, they became full of rage and cried out, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Acts 19:29  The city was filled with confusion. They rushed together into the theater, seizing Gaius and Aristarchus, Macedonians who traveled with Paul.
Acts 19:30  Paul wanted to enter among the populace, but the disciples would not let him.
Acts 19:31  Even some of the Asiarchs, who were his friends, sent to him and urged him not to venture into the theater.
Acts 19:32  Some shouted one thing and some another, for the assembly was confused, and most did not know why they had come together.
Acts 19:33  They prompted Alexander from the crowd, the Jews having put him forward. Alexander motioned with his hand and wished to make a defense before the populace.
Acts 19:34  When they recognized that he was a Jew, one cry arose from them all for about two hours: “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!”
Acts 19:35  The city secretary quieted the crowd and said, “Men of Ephesus, who among human beings does not know that the city of the Ephesians is temple-keeper of the great Artemis and of what fell from Zeus?
Acts 19:36  Since these things are undeniable, you must remain calm and do nothing rash.
Acts 19:37  For you have brought these men here, though they are neither temple-robbers nor blasphemers of our goddess.
Acts 19:38  If Demetrius and the craftsmen with him have a charge against anyone, court sessions are held and proconsuls are available; let them bring charges against one another.
Acts 19:39  But if you seek anything further, it will be settled in the lawful assembly.
Acts 19:40a  For we are in danger of being charged with rioting over today’s events, since there is no cause for it; we will not be able to give an account of this gathering.”
Acts 19:40b  After saying these things, he dismissed the assembly.

Acts 20
Acts 20:1  After the uproar ceased, Paul summoned the disciples and encouraged them. Taking leave of them, he departed for Macedonia.
Acts 20:2  He passed through those regions and encouraged them with many words, then came to Greece
Acts 20:3  and spent three months there. When a plot was made against him by the Jews as he was about to sail for Syria, he decided to return through Macedonia.
Acts 20:4  He was accompanied by Sopater son of Pyrrhus from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus from Thessalonica; Gaius from Derbe, and Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus from Asia.
Acts 20:5  These men went ahead and waited for us in Troas.
Acts 20:6  We sailed from Philippi after the days of Unleavened Bread and came to them at Troas in five days, where we stayed seven days.
Acts 20:7  On the first day of the week, when we had gathered to break bread, Paul spoke with them. He intended to leave the next day and prolonged his message until midnight.
Acts 20:8  There were many lamps in the upper room where we had gathered.
Acts 20:9  A young man named Eutychus sat in the window and was sinking into a deep sleep as Paul continued speaking at length. Overcome by sleep, he fell down from the third story and was picked up dead.
Acts 20:10  Paul went down, fell upon him, embraced him, and said, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.”
Acts 20:11  He went back up, broke the bread and ate, and talked for a long time until dawn. Then he departed.
Acts 20:12  They brought the boy away alive and were greatly comforted.
Acts 20:13  We went ahead to the ship and sailed for Assos, intending to take Paul aboard there, for he had arranged it this way, intending himself to travel on foot.
Acts 20:14  When he met us at Assos, we took him aboard and came to Mitylene.
Acts 20:15  Sailing from there, the next day we arrived opposite Chios; on the following day we put in at Samos, and on the next we came to Miletus.
Acts 20:16  For Paul had decided to sail past Ephesus so that he would not spend time in Asia. He was hurrying, if possible, to be in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost.
Acts 20:17  From Miletus he sent to Ephesus and summoned the elders of the Church.
Acts 20:18  When they came to him, he said, “You know how I was with you the whole time, from the first day I set foot in Asia,
Acts 20:19  serving the Lord with all humility, tears, and trials that came upon me through the plots of the Jews.
Acts 20:20  I did not hold back from declaring anything beneficial to you and teaching you publicly and from house to house,
Acts 20:21  bearing solemn witness to both Jews and Greeks of repentance toward God and faith in our Lord Jesus.
Acts 20:22  And now, look, bound in spirit, I am going to Jerusalem, not knowing what will meet me there,
Acts 20:23  except that in every city the Holy Spirit bears witness to me, saying that bonds and afflictions await me.
Acts 20:24  But I consider my life of no value to myself, so that I may complete my course and the ministry I received from the Lord Jesus: to bear solemn witness to the good news of God’s grace.
Acts 20:25  And now, look, I know that none of you among whom I went about proclaiming the kingdom will see my face again.
Acts 20:26  Therefore I testify to you this very day that I am clean from the blood of all,
Acts 20:27  for I did not hold back from declaring to you the whole purpose of God.
Acts 20:28  Pay attention to yourselves and to all the flock, among whom the Holy Spirit has placed you as overseers, to shepherd the Church of God, which He acquired through His own blood.
Acts 20:29  I know that after my departure fierce wolves will enter among you, not sparing the flock.
Acts 20:30  Even from among you yourselves men will arise, speaking distorted things to draw the disciples away after themselves.
Acts 20:31  Therefore stay awake, remembering that for three years, night and day, I never ceased admonishing each one with tears.
Acts 20:32  And now I entrust you to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up and give you the inheritance among all who have been sanctified.
Acts 20:33  I coveted no one’s silver or gold or clothing.
Acts 20:34  You yourselves know that these hands served my needs and those of the people with me.
Acts 20:35  In everything I showed you that by working in this way we must support the weak and remember the words of the Lord Jesus, that He Himself said, ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’”
Acts 20:36  After saying these things, he knelt down with them all and prayed.
Acts 20:37  They all wept greatly, threw their arms around Paul’s neck, and kissed him repeatedly,
Acts 20:38  grieving most of all over the word he had spoken, that they would no longer see his face. They accompanied him to the ship.

Acts 21
Acts 21:1  When we had torn ourselves away from them and set sail, we made a straight course to Cos, the next day to Rhodes, and from there to Patara.
Acts 21:2  We found a ship crossing to Phoenicia, went aboard, and set sail.
Acts 21:3  We sighted Cyprus and passed it on our left, sailed toward Syria, and landed at Tyre, for the ship was to unload its cargo there.
Acts 21:4  We sought out the disciples and stayed there seven days. Through the Spirit they told Paul not to set foot in Jerusalem.
Acts 21:5  When our days there were completed, we left and went on our way. They all accompanied us, with wives and children, as far as outside the city. We knelt on the beach and prayed,
Acts 21:6  then said farewell to one another. We boarded the ship, and they returned to their homes.
Acts 21:7  Completing the voyage from Tyre, we arrived at Ptolemais, greeted the brothers, and stayed with them for one day.
Acts 21:8  The next day we departed and came to Caesarea. We entered the house of Philip the evangelist, who was one of the seven, and stayed with him.
Acts 21:9  He had four daughters who were virgins and prophesied.
Acts 21:10  While we stayed for several days, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea.
Acts 21:11  He came to us, took Paul’s belt, bound his own feet and hands, and said, “Thus says the Holy Spirit: ‘The Jews in Jerusalem will bind the man whose belt this is in this way and hand him over into Gentile hands.’”
Acts 21:12  When we heard these things, both we and the local people urged him not to go up to Jerusalem.
Acts 21:13  Then Paul answered, “What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart? For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
Acts 21:14  Since he would not be persuaded, we became silent and said, “Let the Lord’s will be done.”
Acts 21:15  After these days we made our preparations and went up to Jerusalem.
Acts 21:16  Some disciples from Caesarea also went with us, taking us to a certain Mnason of Cyprus, an early disciple, with whom we were to lodge.
Acts 21:17  When we arrived in Jerusalem, the brothers welcomed us gladly.
Acts 21:18  The next day Paul went with us to James, and all the elders were present.
Acts 21:19  After greeting them, he related one by one the things God had done among the Gentiles through his ministry.
Acts 21:20  When they heard, they glorified God and said to him, “You see, brother, how many tens of thousands of Jews have believed, and they are all zealous for the law.
Acts 21:21  They have been informed about you that you teach all the Jews among the Gentiles to forsake Moses, telling them not to circumcise their children or walk in the customs.
Acts 21:22  What, then, is to be done? They will certainly hear that you have come.
Acts 21:23  Therefore do what we tell you. We have four men who have taken a vow upon themselves.
Acts 21:24  Take these men, purify yourself with them, and pay their expenses so that they may shave their heads. Then everyone will know that there is nothing to what they have been told about you, but that you yourself also walk in step, keeping the law.
Acts 21:25  But concerning the Gentiles who have believed, we have sent word, judging that they should keep themselves from what is sacrificed to idols, blood, what is strangled, and sexual immorality.”
Acts 21:26  Then Paul took the men, and on the next day, after purifying himself with them, he entered the temple, giving notice of the completion of the days of purification, up to the presentation of the offering for each one of them.
Acts 21:27  When the seven days were about to be completed, the Jews from Asia saw him in the temple, stirred up the whole crowd, and laid hands on him,
Acts 21:28  crying, “Men of Israel, help! This is the man who teaches everyone everywhere against the people, the law, and this place. Moreover, he has even brought Greeks into the temple and defiled this holy place.”
Acts 21:29  For they had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city and supposed that Paul had brought him into the temple.
Acts 21:30  The whole city was stirred, and the people ran together. They seized Paul and dragged him outside the temple, and immediately the doors were shut.
Acts 21:31  While they were seeking to kill him, a report reached the tribune of the cohort that all Jerusalem was in confusion.
Acts 21:32  He immediately took soldiers and centurions and ran down to them. When they saw the tribune and the soldiers, they stopped beating Paul.
Acts 21:33  Then the tribune approached, seized him, and ordered him bound with two chains. He asked who he was and what he had done.
Acts 21:34  Some in the crowd shouted one thing and some another. Since he could learn nothing certain because of the uproar, he ordered Paul to be brought into the barracks.
Acts 21:35  When he reached the steps, the soldiers had to carry him because of the crowd’s violence,
Acts 21:36  for the multitude of the people followed, crying, “Away with him!”
Acts 21:37  As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he said to the tribune, “May I say something to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek?
Acts 21:38  Then are you not the Egyptian who some time ago stirred up a revolt and led the four thousand men of the Sicarii into the wilderness?”
Acts 21:39  Paul said, “I am a Jewish man from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no insignificant city. I ask you, allow me to speak to the people.”
Acts 21:40  When he gave permission, Paul stood on the steps and motioned with his hand to the people. When a great silence fell, he addressed them in the Hebrew language, saying:

Acts 22
Acts 22:1  “Men, brothers and fathers, hear the defense I now make before you.”
Acts 22:2  When they heard that he addressed them in the Hebrew language, they became still quieter. He said:
Acts 22:3  “I am a Jewish man, born in Tarsus of Cilicia, but brought up in this city at the feet of Gamaliel, educated in the strict observance of the ancestral law, zealous for God as all of you are today.
Acts 22:4  I persecuted this Way to the point of death, binding and handing over to prisons both men and women,
Acts 22:5  as the high priest and the whole council of elders can testify for me. From them I also received letters to the brothers, and I went toward Damascus to bring those there bound to Jerusalem for punishment.
Acts 22:6  As I was traveling and drawing near Damascus, about noon, a brilliant light from heaven suddenly flashed around me.
Acts 22:7  I fell to the ground and heard a voice saying to me, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting Me?’
Acts 22:8  I answered, ‘Who art Thou, Lord?’ He said to me, ‘I am Jesus the Nazarene, whom you are persecuting.’
Acts 22:9  Those with me saw the light, but they did not hear the voice of the One speaking to me.
Acts 22:10  I said, ‘What should I do, Lord?’ The Lord said to me, ‘Rise and go into Damascus, and there you will be told about everything appointed for you to do.’
Acts 22:11  Since I could not see because of the brightness of that light, I was led by the hand by those with me and came into Damascus.
Acts 22:12  A certain Ananias, a man devout according to the law and well spoken of by all the Jews living there,
Acts 22:13  came to me, stood beside me, and said, ‘Brother Saul, regain your sight.’ At that very hour I regained my sight and looked at him.
Acts 22:14  He said, ‘The God of our fathers appointed you to know His will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear a voice from His mouth,
Acts 22:15  for you will be His witness to all people of what you have seen and heard.
Acts 22:16  Now why do you delay? Rise, be baptized, and wash away your sins, calling upon His name.’
Acts 22:17  After I returned to Jerusalem, while I was praying in the temple, I fell into a trance
Acts 22:18  and saw Him saying to me, ‘Hurry, and go out quickly from Jerusalem, because they will not accept your testimony about Me.’
Acts 22:19  I said, ‘Lord, they themselves know that I used to imprison and beat in the synagogues those who believe in Thee.
Acts 22:20  And when the blood of Stephen, Thy witness, was being poured out, I myself stood by, approving and guarding the garments of those who were killing him.’
Acts 22:21  He said to me, ‘Go, for I will send you far away to the Gentiles.’”
Acts 22:22  They listened to him until this statement, then raised their voice and said, “Remove such a man from the earth, for he ought not to live.”
Acts 22:23  As they shouted, flung their garments, and threw dust into the air,
Acts 22:24  the tribune ordered him brought into the barracks and directed that he be examined by scourging, so that he might learn why they were shouting against him in this way.
Acts 22:25  As they stretched him out with the straps, Paul said to the centurion standing nearby, “Is it lawful for you to scourge a Roman citizen who has not been condemned?”
Acts 22:26  When the centurion heard this, he went to the tribune and reported it, saying, “What are you about to do? This man is a Roman.”
Acts 22:27  The tribune came and said to him, “Tell me, are you a Roman?” He said, “Yes.”
Acts 22:28  The tribune answered, “I acquired this citizenship for a large sum.” Paul said, “But I was born with it.”
Acts 22:29  Those about to examine him immediately withdrew. The tribune too was afraid when he learned that Paul was a Roman and that he had bound him.
Acts 22:30  The next day, wishing to learn with certainty what accusation the Jews were bringing against him, he unbound him and ordered the chief priests and the whole council to assemble. He brought Paul down and set him before them.

Acts 23
Acts 23:1  Paul looked intently at the council and said, “Men, brothers, I have conducted my life before God with an entirely good conscience to this day.”
Acts 23:2  The high priest Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike his mouth.
Acts 23:3  Then Paul said to him, “God is going to strike you, whitewashed wall! You sit judging me according to the law, yet in violation of the law you order me struck?”
Acts 23:4  Those standing nearby said, “Are you insulting God’s high priest?”
Acts 23:5  Paul said, “Brothers, I did not know that he was high priest, for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people.’”
